extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent agents, and patentees involved in infringement actions (primarily UK practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on procedural and evidentiary rules in actions for patent infringement: interlocutory injunctions, consolidation, discovery/inspection, particulars of breaches/objections, trial practice, and evaluation of evidence (UK context, Patents Act 1883 and related rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting interlocutory injunctions — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court will grant an interlocutory injunction (before trial) where a patent has been granted and there has been exclusive possession of some duration; but where the patent is recent and its validity is contested (e.g., bad specification), the Court will not grant an injunction without the patentee first establishing validity at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court weighs presumed validity against opposing evidence; when patent is 'of yesterday' and validity is attacked, send patentee to law to establish validity before granting injunction. See Lord Eldon in Hill v. Thompson and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors favouring interlocutory injunction — long undisturbed enjoyment / established validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee has had long, undisputed enjoyment of the patent, or where validity has been established elsewhere, the Court can grant an interlocutory injunction even without a full trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (e.g., Dudgeon v. Thomson) indicate Court may act when it 'sees no reason to doubt the propriety of the result' or where conduct of defendant leaves no reason to doubt validity. Multiple prior suits decided for patentee also support granting injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to show actual public user for reliance on long possession
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on long and undisputed possession as ground for an interlocutory injunction, the patentee must show actual public user of the invention, unfettered by necessity of obtaining licences of prior patentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (e.g., Chippman v. Nielson; Walker v. Mullin) require evidence of public user and lack of subordination to prior rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay or negligence in prosecuting rights affects injunction relief
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff has shown negligence or undue delay in prosecuting his rights, an interim injunction will be refused, though delay may be excused if satisfactorily explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if validity was previously established, negligence in enforcement can bar interim relief (cases cited). Court may grant injunction if delay is satisfactorily explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction refusal where infringement is doubtful; accounting as interim measure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the fact of infringement is doubtful, the Court will refuse an injunction until after trial; nevertheless the Court often orders the defendant to keep an account pending determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where issue is doubtful, injunction refused; but Court 'postpones' consideration and may require accounting until plaintiff tests validity. If injunction granted, plaintiff must give undertaking as to damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's undertaking as condition of interlocutory injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: When an interlocutory injunction is granted the Court requires the plaintiff to give an undertaking to abide by any order as to damages if it later finds the defendant suffered loss by the injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard condition in equity — plaintiff liable for damages if ultimately injunction was wrong (cases: Wakefield v. Duke of Buccleuch; United Telephone Co. v. Equitable Telephone Association).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's current reluctance to grant interlocutory injunctions where validity can be tried
rubrics_metrics.description: Since courts are empowered to try patent validity and control proceedings, they are less disposed to grant interlocutory injunctions (especially for new patents) and prefer to direct immediate trial of issues, possibly ordering accounting instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may add directions to insure immediate trial and order the motion for injunction to stand to the hearing of the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction where defendant shows intention to infringe (anticipatory manufacture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court may grant an injunction even absent actual infringement where the defendant has shown intention and means to infringe (e.g., secretly manufacturing copies to flood market upon expiry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: injunction to restrain use even after patent expiry where defendant secretly manufactured infringing articles before expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of multiple actions against separate infringers
rubrics_metrics.description: When plaintiff commences multiple actions against separate infringers, the Court may order that validity and common questions be tried in one action and stay others — but only after defendants give full discovery of the machines/processes alleged to infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order will not be made until defendants have given full discovery; plaintiff is not bound by an adverse result in the chosen action and may proceed against others unless prevented by order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical issues in a patent action
rubrics_metrics.description: Common issues raised (and which may be settled as issues of fact) include whether the invention is new, whether it is useful, whether it was a new manufacture, whether the patentee was the true and first inventor, whether the specification is sufficient, and whether the defendant has infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues can be varied as circumstances require; since Judicature Acts practice tends to let action come on for trial generally upon pleadings and particulars rather than by formal issues application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection of machines/processes (order under Patents Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under s.30 of the Patents Act 1883 the Court or judge may, on application of either party, make orders for injunction, inspection, or account and impose terms and directions as seen fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspection was historically ordered in many cases; Supreme Court Rules also empower taking samples, observations, experiments to obtain full information or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeeping for inspection — necessity and sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspection will not be granted unless the Court is satisfied there is really a case to be tried and that inspection is essential to enable the plaintiff to prove his case; orders are refused where evidence of infringement amounts only to suspicion and grounds are not stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: rejected when mere suspicion (Y/wit Milling Co. v. Pinhinton). Inspection may be ordered where essential and well-founded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of inspection — examples and practical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Court may limit inspection requests to what is reasonable — e.g., refuse broad orders to inspect all machines, but direct defendant to verify kinds sold and produce representative samples at solicitor's office for inspection by plaintiff's experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order tailored to avoid fishing expeditions; court may require production of one of each class and allow expert inspection (Manufacturing Co. v. Wilson; Drake v. Muntz's Metal Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee not compellable to give inspection in action against licensor
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who is not a party to the action cannot be compelled to give inspection in an action against his licensor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Germ Milling Co. v. Robinson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars of breaches — statutory requirement and amendability
rubrics_metrics.description: By Patents Act 1883 s.29 the plaintiff must deliver particulars of the breaches with his statement of claim (or later by order); particulars may be amended by leave of the Court or judge and further/better particulars may be required if insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particulars are sufficient if, together with the pleadings, they give the defendant full and fair notice of the case (Needham v. Oxley); the Court may order pointing to pages/lines of specification when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointing to specification pages/lines where required
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may be ordered to point out by reference to pages and lines the parts of specification alleged to be infringed, but this is not required when the infringing articles are exhibits or when particulars and claims already enable defendant to know what he will have to meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court exercises discretion based on what suffices to give clear notice (Lamb v. The Nottingham Manufacturers' Co.; Batley v. Kynock; Cheetham v. Oldham).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars of objections by defendant — requirements and amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant must deliver particulars of objections with his statement of defence (Patents Act s.29); if disputing validity, he must state grounds, and if want of novelty is alleged, he must state time and place of prior publication or user; particulars may be amended by leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant should indicate whether relying on general public knowledge or on specific publications as anticipations — different detail required for each. Subsection allows amendment from time to time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing general public knowledge from anticipatory publications
rubrics_metrics.description: If relying on general public knowledge, defendant should not enumerate books/publications in particulars; public knowledge must be proved by witnesses and may refer to well-known books at trial. If relying on particular publications as anticipations, defendant must identify the publications, where found, the nature of the anticipation, and indicate reliance as anticipation (not general knowledge); indicate relevant claim if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may require striking out publications that only show public knowledge; pages/lines need not be given unless matter would be doubtful without them (Holliday v. Heppenstall). Earlier practice sometimes demanded pages/lines; modern practice more flexible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on particulars — objections cannot go beyond pleas
rubrics_metrics.description: Particulars of objections are to state more particularly what the pleas state generally and cannot go beyond the pleas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Macnamara v. Hulse and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave to amend particulars — timing and costs considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave to amend particulars of breaches or objections may be granted under special circumstances, including even on the eve of trial or during trial (with adjournment); the Court considers timing and may address costs in the order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases consider amendments on eve of trial, during trial, and the form of order as to costs (e.g., Parke v. Muirton's Filter Co.; Hlabin v. Lathen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatories — scope in infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant denying infringement may be compelled to answer whether he used the plaintiff's materials, whether he makes any addition to them, and whether such addition makes any difference; limits of discovery governed by case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Gernard v. ?; Crossley v. Steelcraft; Lister v. ?; and extensive authorities referenced. Plaintiff may also be interrogated about documents relating to preparation of specification (Moseley v. Victoria Rubber Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery after particulars — names/addresses and existence of machines
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who has furnished particulars in compliance with the statute may be called upon to answer interrogatories as to names and addresses of alleged prior users and whether the machines are in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example authority: Birch v. Mather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order for production of models — possession/power requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Order for production of models, dies, drawings before trial will be refused if articles are not shown to be in the possession or power of the defendants; judge has no jurisdiction to compel production of articles not in defendant's control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garrard v. Edge: production refused where not in possession/power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection of documents — privilege and patent agent communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications between an inventor and his patent agent are not privileged; where patent agent is also solicitor, communications made to him in capacity of patent agent may be inspected if no other valid objection to disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moseley v. Victoria Rubber Co. held defendants entitled to inspect communications bearing on preparation of specification when relevant to infringement dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documents prepared for litigation — possible protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents which plaintiffs state on oath came into existence merely to be communicated to their solicitor for purpose of litigation, or as materials for briefs, may be excluded from inspection; otherwise defendants may be entitled to inspect documents relating to prior validity disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court distinguished litigation-only documents from other relevant documents (Chitlain Co. v. Hall). In amalgamation cases, particulars from prior litigation may be subject to inspection (Edison & Swan v. Holland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial procedures — judge, jury, referee, and assessor
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions are to be tried without a jury unless Court otherwise directs (Patents Act). Judge may send issues requiring 'scientific investigation' to a referee; Court may call in an assessor specially qualified and try or hear case with his assistance; remuneration of assessor determined by Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitration Act 1889 and Judicature Act provisions allow referee for scientific issues; findings of referee equivalent to jury. Court may order competent person to make experiments and report for Court's guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's power to allow amendment at Patent Office and postpone trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge is empowered (by statutory provision cited) in an infringement or revocation action to give liberty to the patentee to apply at the Patent Office for leave to amend his specification and to postpone the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See chapter on Amendments; judge has discretion to allow amendment and adjournment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret processes — in camera handling
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant asserting a secret process may be permitted not to answer certain questions in open court to avoid irreparable mischief; judge may hear description in private (closed doors) with only parties and scientific assistants present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: defendant allowed to disclose secret to judge in camera (Badische Anilin und Soda Fabrik v. Levinstein; Kilburn v. ?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Models in court for illustration (not formally in evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A model not put in evidence may nevertheless be handed up to the Court as an example of a class of machine to explain counsel's argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for illustration of argument (Goodliffe v. Hockings, Appeal authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial respect for prior trial findings on validity/usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a judge at trial is of opinion that the invention is good subject-matter and useful and upholds patent on these respects, his decision will be followed by another judge of coordinate jurisdiction if identical grounds are later contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency across co-ordinate judges; see cited cases (6 R.P.C. authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's approach to evidence — distrust manufactured experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court looks with distrust on experiments conducted for the express purpose of manufacturing evidence for the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities warn against admitting experiments prepared solely to support litigation (Young v. Fernie; Betts v. Neilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence limited to particulars — leave required for additional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: By s.29(4) of the Act of 1883, no evidence is to be admitted at the hearing except by leave of the Court or a judge in proof of any alleged infringement or objection of which particulars have not been delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court has discretionary power to allow evidence beyond particulars; may allow evidence of additional sales etc. where defendant admits relevant conduct (Britain v. Hirsch; Sykes v. Howarth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Onus of proof for lack of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: In infringement actions the onus of proof of want of novelty lies on the defendant; therefore, in an uncontested case the plaintiff is not bound to prove novelty of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Peroni v. Hudson — defendant must prove anticipation; plaintiff may rely on presumption absent contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's right to adduce evidence in reply
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff is entitled to adduce evidence in reply for the purpose of rebutting the case set up by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard right to reply evidence to meet defendant's case (Jervis v. Jack).
